# Chapter Review

## Flashcards
<FlashcardDeck>
  <Flashcard front="What is the sum of the geometric series $1 + 2 + 4 + ... + N$?" back="Approximately $2N$, which simplifies to $\mathcal{O}(N)$." />
  <Flashcard front="In the Aggregate Method, how do you find amortized cost?" back="Divide the total worst-case cost of $M$ operations by $M$." />
  <Flashcard front="If $T(n) = T(n-1) + \mathcal{O}(1)$, what is the complexity?" back="$\mathcal{O}(N)$, because it expands to a simple sum of $N$ constants." />
</FlashcardDeck>

## Quick Quiz
<Quiz
  title="Chapter 2 Quick Check"
  questions={[
    {
      question: "Which case of the Master Theorem applies to $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + \mathcal{O}(n)$?",
      options: ["Case 1", "Case 2", "Case 3", "Master Theorem does not apply"],
      correctIndex: 1,
      explanation: "$n^{\log_2 2} = n^1$. $f(n) = \mathcal{O}(n)$. Since they are equal, it's Case 2, resulting in $\mathcal{O}(n \log n)$."
    }
  ]}
/>

# Chapter Review

## Flashcards
<FlashcardDeck>
  <Flashcard front="What is the time complexity of generating all valid parentheses of $N$ pairs?" back="$\mathcal{O}(4^N / \sqrt{N})$, which is the $N$th Catalan number." />
  <Flashcard front="In D&C, what happens if the left and right halves return different majority candidates?" back="You must count the exact occurrences of both candidates in the full array to see if either exceeds $N/2$." />
  <Flashcard front="What is the key difference between Memoization and Tabulation?" back="Memoization is top-down (recursive with caching), Tabulation is bottom-up (iterative table filling)." />
</FlashcardDeck>

# Chapter Review

## Flashcards
<FlashcardDeck>
  <Flashcard front="What is the time complexity of reversing a linked list in blocks of $K$?" back="$\mathcal{O}(N)$, because each node is visited and swapped a constant number of times." />
  <Flashcard front="In Shunting Yard, how do you handle right-associative operators like $\wedge$?" back="You only pop from the stack if the incoming operator has strictly GREATER precedence, not equal." />
  <Flashcard front="Why does a circular array of size $N$ only hold $N-1$ elements if we don't use a size counter?" back="To distinguish between the 'empty' state ($front == rear$) and the 'full' state ($rear$ wraps around to $front$)." />
</FlashcardDeck>

## Quick Quiz
<Quiz
  title="Chapter 4 Quick Check"
  questions={[
    {
      question: "When evaluating a postfix expression, what happens when you encounter an operator?",
      options: ["Push it to the stack", "Pop one operand and apply", "Pop two operands, apply, and push result", "Clear the stack"],
      correctIndex: 2,
      explanation: "Postfix evaluation requires two operands for any binary operator. You pop the top two, compute, and push the result back."
    }
  ]}
/>

# Chapter Review

## Flashcards
<FlashcardDeck>
  <Flashcard front="What method do you use in Java to chain multiple sorting criteria?" back="thenComparing() or thenComparingDouble(), etc." />
  <Flashcard front="Why does Binary Search degrade to $\mathcal{O}(N)$ on a rotated array with many duplicates?" back="When $arr[mid] == arr[high]$, you cannot determine which side is sorted, forcing a linear step to shrink the search space." />
  <Flashcard front="What is the main advantage of LSD Radix sort over MSD Radix sort?" back="LSD can be implemented iteratively and naturally handles variable-length strings/numbers by padding." />
</FlashcardDeck>

## Quick Quiz
<Quiz
  title="Chapter 5 Quick Check"
  questions={[
    {
      question: "In Quick Sort, what is the primary purpose of the Median-of-Three pivot selection?",
      options: ["To guarantee $\mathcal{O}(N \log N)$ worst-case time", "To prevent $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ degradation on already sorted arrays", "To reduce space complexity to $\mathcal{O}(1)$", "To make the sort stable"],
      correctIndex: 1,
      explanation: "It avoids picking the absolute minimum or maximum as the pivot when the array is already sorted, which causes the worst-case partitioning."
    }
  ]}
/>

# Chapter Review

## Flashcards
<FlashcardDeck>
  <Flashcard front="When deleting a BST node with two children, what is the in-order predecessor?" back="The maximum value in the node's left subtree." />
  <Flashcard front="What is the time complexity to build a heap from an unsorted array (heapify)?" back="$\mathcal{O}(N)$, not $\mathcal{O}(N \log N)$, due to the mathematical sum of heights." />
  <Flashcard front="In a Trie, what does the `isEndOfWord` boolean signify?" back="It marks that the path from root to this node forms a complete, valid word, not just a prefix." />
</FlashcardDeck>

## Quick Quiz
<Quiz
  title="Chapter 6 Quick Check"
  questions={[
    {
      question: "If an AVL tree node has a balance factor of -2 and its right child has a balance factor of +1, which rotation is needed?",
      options: ["Left-Left (Single Right)", "Right-Right (Single Left)", "Right-Left (Double)", "Left-Right (Double)"],
      correctIndex: 2,
      explanation: "The node is right-heavy (-2), but the right child is left-heavy (+1). This requires a Right rotation on the child, followed by a Left rotation on the node."

# Chapter Review

## Flashcards
<FlashcardDeck>
  <Flashcard front="What is a 'Tombstone' in Open Addressing?" back="A special marker placed in a deleted slot that tells search to keep probing, but tells insert that the slot is available." />
  <Flashcard front="How do you compute a Zobrist hash for a new chess board state?" back="By XORing the pre-generated random numbers for every piece currently occupying a square on the board." />
  <Flashcard front="Can you delete an element from a Bloom Filter?" back="No, because clearing a bit might accidentally delete a bit required by a different element that shares that hash index." />
</FlashcardDeck>

## Quick Quiz
<Quiz
  title="Chapter 7 Quick Check"
  questions={[
    {
      question: "In Separate Chaining, what happens when the load factor exceeds the threshold?",
      options: ["The oldest elements are evicted", "A rehash is triggered to double the array capacity", "The linked lists are converted to binary search trees", "The hash function is changed"],
      correctIndex: 1,
      explanation: "To maintain $\mathcal{O}(1)$ amortized operations, the underlying array is doubled in size and all existing elements are re-inserted using the new modulo base."
    }
  ]}

# Chapter Review

## Flashcards
<FlashcardDeck>
  <Flashcard front="How do you reconstruct a path after running BFS?" back="Use a HashMap to store the 'parent' of each visited node, then backtrack from the target to the source." />
  <Flashcard front="Why does Dijkstra fail when edges have secondary constraints (like a toll budget)?" back="Because the optimal substructure property is broken; a longer path might preserve budget needed for later edges." />
  <Flashcard front="In Kahn's Algorithm, how do you know if the graph contains a cycle?" back="If the number of nodes processed (popped from queue) is less than the total number of vertices in the graph." />
</FlashcardDeck>

## Quick Quiz
<Quiz
  title="Chapter 8 Quick Check"
  questions={[
    {
      question: "In Kruskal's algorithm, what data structure is used to efficiently detect cycles?",
      options: ["Priority Queue", "Adjacency Matrix", "Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find)", "Stack"],
      correctIndex: 2,
      explanation: "DSU allows near $\mathcal{O}(1)$ checks to see if two vertices belong to the same connected component, which prevents forming a cycle."
    }
  ]}
/>
